When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is why women need to perform self-exams regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change. Of course talking about breast cancer and breast health is a personal thing. I too am a private person but encourage all women to break through their reservations and talk to their doctors and physicians. We must also banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who were diagnosed in their 20s, an age when most women are graduating from college and just starting their lives as full adults.  Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk » . Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years and women 40 and older should have an exam every year. I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, myself, my children and future generations of women, so one day we will not have to be afraid of breast cancer. I began my fight by learning important first steps in breast cancer detection, and will not end my fight until every woman can stand together saying we are breast cancer free. More than anything else, I have faith -- faith we will find a cure. **(CNN)** — Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic terrifying. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing this figure placed it all into sobering perspective.

Women close to me have battled the disease and are now soldiers in the greater fight against it. Yet the moment I heard "every three minutes," I felt vulnerable and afraid, realizing that no one is immune. The only way to ease my fears was to take action. I needed to educate myself and others about this disease. As the Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation, I had invaluable resources at my fingertips. I had access to an entire organization devoted to giving back to women and educating the public. So I began to ask, "What do I need to know?"

It was through that curiosity that I discovered the most important fact about breast cancer: early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, there is a 97 percent five-year survival rate when breast cancer is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body. When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is precisely why women must perform self-examinations regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the slightest change.

Of course, discussing breast cancer and breast health is a deeply personal matter. I, too, am a private person, but I encourage all women to overcome their reservations and speak openly with their doctors and physicians.

We must also dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. **Editor's Note:** Reese Witherspoon, who has won an Academy Award for her acting, serves as honorary chairman of the Avon Foundation and works for Avon Products in the role of global ambassador. Here, Witherspoon explains her desire to dispel the false belief that breast cancer poses no threat to young women.

(CNN) -- In America, a woman receives a breast cancer diagnosis once every three minutes. Being a woman, a mother, and a daughter myself, I find that number absolutely frightening. While I was always aware of breast cancer, learning this figure gave me a whole new understanding of its reality.

I have watched women I love fight this illness, and today they stand as warriors in the broader campaign against it. Yet the instant I heard those words—"every three minutes"—a wave of fear and vulnerability washed over me as it dawned on me that no one is immune. For me, the only path to calming that fear was to do something. I had to teach myself and others about this illness. Serving as the Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation meant I had answers within reach. An entire organization committed to supporting women and spreading awareness was available to me. So I began to ask, "What is it I should know?"

That very curiosity led me to discover the single most crucial truth about breast cancer: catching it early saves lives. Data from the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade shows a 97 percent survival rate over five years when the disease is identified before reaching other areas of the body. In its early stages, breast cancer typically produces no warning signs at all, which is precisely why women should routinely examine themselves and reach out to their doctor the moment they detect even a tiny difference.

Naturally, discussing breast cancer and breast health feels deeply personal. I'm a private individual myself, yet I urge every woman to overcome her hesitations and speak openly with her doctors and physicians.

We also have to put an end to the false notion that breast cancer doesn't threaten younger women. During the Avon Walk in Washington, I encountered young survivors whose diagnoses came in their 20s—a time when most women are finishing college and only beginning their adult lives. Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »

Women in their 20s and 30s ought to receive a clinical breast exam from a medical professional no less than once every three years, while those 40 and up should be examined annually.

I feel deeply committed to battling this terrible disease. My fight is for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for the women who will come after us, so that someday breast cancer will no longer be something we fear. I launched my own fight by mastering the essential early measures for detecting breast cancer, and I refuse to stop until every woman can join together and declare herself free of this disease. Above everything, I hold onto faith—faith that a cure will be found.

I witnessed that same dedication written across the faces of the women in Washington—in those who walked and in the women and men lining the route, cheering all 3,500 participants toward the finish. I was cheering alongside them, calling out for the action needed to discover a cure.

The next Avon walk is scheduled for New York City on October 4 and 5.

The reality is sobering. In the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer every three minutes. This staggering statistic underscores a crucial truth—breast cancer does not discriminate. Anyone can be susceptible to the disease, regardless of age or background, making awareness and vigilance essential for every woman.

Perhaps the most important message in the fight against breast cancer is the value of early detection. When the disease is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body, the five-year survival rate reaches an encouraging 97 percent. This remarkable statistic highlights why timely diagnosis is the single most critical factor in successfully combating breast cancer.

However, early detection presents its own challenges, as breast cancer often produces no symptoms in its initial stages. For this reason, women are strongly encouraged to perform regular self-examinations and to remain attentive to their bodies. Even the smallest change should prompt a call to the doctor, as acting quickly can make all the difference in outcomes.

Finally, Witherspoon urges women to overcome any personal reservations they may have about discussing their health. Breast health should never be a taboo subject. **Editor's Note:** *The following is an illustrative, hypothetical op-ed written in the voice of actress and producer Reese Witherspoon, who has served as a Global Ambassador and Honorary Chairman of the Avon Foundation for Women. This piece was composed as a writing sample and does not represent an actual statement authored or endorsed by Ms. Witherspoon. The views expressed are presented for illustrative purposes only.*

---

# We Can't Afford to Wait: Why Breast Cancer Awareness Matters at Every Age

*By Reese Witherspoon*

When people find out about the work I do with the Avon Foundation for Women, they sometimes assume it's just another cause a celebrity lends her name to. A red-carpet ribbon. A photo op. But this work is personal to me, and it has been for a long time.

Like so many families, mine has felt the reach of breast cancer. I've sat with women I love as they've waited for results, watched them navigate treatment with a courage that humbles me, and I've mourned those we've lost. Those experiences changed the way I think about my own health—and about my responsibility to speak up for other women.

That's why I want to say something plainly: **early detection saves lives.** It is not a slogan. It is the difference, for countless women, between a treatable diagnosis and a devastating one.

## The Myth That "It Won't Happen to Me"

For years, I believed breast cancer was something that happened to other people—older people, people with a family history, someone, anyone, other than me and my friends. That belief is dangerous, and it's one I hear echoed by young women all the time.

The truth is that breast cancer does not check your ID. While the risk rises with age, thousands of women in their 20s and 30s are diagnosed every year. Younger women are often diagnosed at later stages, in part because neither they nor their doctors expect it. A lump gets dismissed as "probably nothing." A concern gets waved away because "you're too young to worry."

You are never too young to know your own body. You are never too young to advocate for yourself. And you are never too young to insist that a doctor take your concerns seriously.

## Know Your Normal

Here's the practical part—the part I wish someone had drilled into me when I was younger.

**Know what's normal for you.** Your body is yours, and you are the world's leading expert on it. Pay attention to changes—a lump, a thickening, dimpling of the skin, changes in shape or the nipple, unusual pain. If something feels different, don't wait. Don't second-guess yourself. Make the call.

**Talk to your family.** Understanding your family history can help you and your doctor decide when screening should begin and how often. That conversation might feel awkward. Have it anyway.

**Ask questions—and keep asking.** If you're not satisfied with an answer, seek another. Trusting your instincts is not being difficult. It's being your own best advocate.

## Why the Avon Foundation

What drew me to the Avon Foundation for Women is that it meets women where they are. Through its programs, it has helped fund research, screenings, education, and access to care for women who might otherwise fall through the cracks—including women in underserved communities who face real barriers to a simple screening that could save their lives.

Because let's be honest: awareness alone isn't enough if a woman can't get to a doctor, can't afford a mammogram, or doesn't have anyone telling her that her health matters. Access matters. Education matters. And organizations that fund the science we still desperately need matter.

I've been fortunate to meet survivors, researchers, doctors, and volunteers through this work, and what strikes me every time is how connected we all are in this fight. A grandmother in one town. A college student in another. A single mother working two jobs. Their stories are different, but the message is the same: information and access give women a fighting chance.

## What I'm Asking of You

So here is my ask—and I'm asking it of every woman reading this, and of everyone who loves a woman.

Learn your body. Schedule the appointment you've been putting off. Talk to your mother, your sisters, your daughters, your friends. If you're a young woman who's been told you're "too young to worry," remember that vigilance is not fear—it's power.

And if you have the means to give your time or your support to organizations doing this work, do it. Not next month. Not someday. Now.

I make my living telling stories, and I've learned that the ones that stay with us are the ones about ordinary people finding extraordinary strength. Every woman who catches her cancer early, who advocates for herself, who shows up for a friend in the waiting room—she is that story.

We can't afford to wait. Neither can they.

---

*Reese Witherspoon is an Academy Award–winning actress and producer who has served as a Global Ambassador and Honorary Chairman of the Avon Foundation for Women.*

---

# Don't Wait: Your Life Is Worth the Appointment

*By [Celebrity Author]*

I remember the exact moment my friend told me she'd found a lump. Her voice shook over the phone, and in that instant, everything else in my busy, over-scheduled life fell away. She was one of the lucky ones—she'd caught it early. But her story could have ended very differently, and that's exactly why I'm writing this today.

As someone who has spent years in the public eye, I've learned that a platform comes with responsibility. So I want to use mine to talk about something that affects one in eight women in the United States: breast cancer.

## The Numbers That Should Move Us to Action

Here's what gives me hope: when breast cancer is detected early, before it has spread beyond the breast, the five-year survival rate is remarkably high—around 99 percent. That statistic isn't just a number. It represents mothers who watch their children grow up, friends who show up for decades of birthdays, and women who get to keep writing their stories.

But that survival rate drops significantly when the cancer is found at a later stage. The difference between early and late detection can be the difference between a treatable diagnosis and a devastating one.

Organizations like the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade have long championed this message, funding awareness, access to screening, and research—particularly for underserved women who too often fall through the cracks of our healthcare system. Their work reminds us that early detection saves lives, but only when women have the knowledge and the access to act.

## What You Can Do—Starting Today

Screening guidelines can feel confusing, so let me keep it simple. Talk to your doctor about what's right for you, because your personal risk factors matter. But here are the general principles worth knowing:

- **Know your body.** Familiarize yourself with how your breasts normally look and feel, so you'll notice if something changes.
- **Talk to your doctor about mammograms.** Many guidelines recommend women begin regular mammogram screening in their 40s, with the timing and frequency depending on individual risk. Women with a family history or other risk factors may need to start earlier.
- **Don't ignore changes.** A lump, thickening, skin dimpling, or nipple changes deserve a conversation with your doctor—not a "wait and see."
- **Know your family history.** Genetics can play a significant role, so gather this information and share it with your healthcare provider.

## The Barrier I Want to Break Down

I know why women put this off. We're busy. We're caretakers. We put everyone else first. And for too many women, cost and access are real, painful obstacles. These are the exact barriers that foundations working in this space are fighting to eliminate—because a woman's zip code or income should never determine whether she survives.

But I want to speak directly to the woman who has been meaning to schedule that appointment for months: **Please, make the call.**

The two hours you spend at a screening could give you decades. The awkwardness of an exam is nothing compared to the peace of mind—or the early warning—it can provide.

## For the Women I'll Never Meet

I think about my friend often. Today, she's healthy, cancer-free, and fiercely grateful. She caught it early. I want that outcome for you, for your sister, for your mother, for your best friend.

So here's my ask: After you finish reading this, do two things. Schedule your own screening if you're due for one. Then send this to a woman you love and tell her to do the same.

We can't control everything about our health. But this—this we can act on. And acting could save your life.

*[Celebrity Author] is an actor and advocate who supports women's health initiatives. The views expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author.*

---

**A note on the guidelines:** *Screening recommendations vary among health organizations and evolve as research advances. Always consult your personal physician about the screening schedule that's right for you.*

# The Miles We Walk Together

There is a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. I know that moment well. I have stood in it countless times—in hospital corridors, in quiet kitchens holding a cup of coffee gone cold, in the hushed space between hope and fear. It is in that moment that I remember why I do this work, why I lend my name and my heart to this fight against breast cancer.

They call me an award-winning actress. They place a golden statue in my hands and ask me to smile for cameras. But the role that has meant the most to me is one no script ever prepared me for: witness. Advocate. Sister to millions of women I will never meet but whose stories live inside me like a second heartbeat.

## What the Statistics Cannot Tell You

We speak of breast cancer in numbers—one in eight women, thousands of diagnoses, survival rates rising and falling like tides. But numbers are cold comfort when the woman in question is your own mother, your daughter, your dearest friend. Numbers cannot capture the sound of a strong woman's voice cracking as she says the word "malignant" for the first time. Numbers cannot show you the way a family reorganizes itself around a single, terrifying appointment.

I have held the hands of women in treatment centers whose courage put my own to shame. I have watched them laugh through fear, comfort their frightened children, and find grace in the most ungraceful of circumstances. These women—these ordinary, extraordinary women—are the reason I cannot stay silent. They are the reason I refuse to.

## Why I Walk

Every year, I lace up my shoes and join thousands of others on the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer, and I am reminded that this fight was never meant to be waged alone. There is something sacred about putting one foot in front of the other alongside strangers who become family over the course of those long, blister-inducing miles.

We walk in memory of those we have lost. We walk in honor of those still fighting. We walk for the ones who cannot walk themselves—the women too weakened by treatment, the women waiting for results, the women whose names we will never know but whose futures depend on the research and support that every step helps fund.

I have seen survivors walking with pink sashes draped across their shoulders like badges of a battle hard-won. I have seen husbands walking for wives they lost too soon, their faces etched with a grief that time softens but never erases. I have seen young daughters walking beside mothers in remission, terrified of a future they cannot control but determined to face it standing up. Each of them carries a story. Each of them walks so that fewer stories will end in heartbreak.

## The Personal Truth

I will tell you something I do not often share. My motivation is not abstract. It is not born from a press release or a well-managed cause. It comes from watching someone I loved fade before her time, from feeling utterly powerless as illness took what medicine could not yet save.

That powerlessness transformed into purpose. I decided that if I could not save her, I would fight for the countless women who could still be saved. Fame is a strange and fleeting thing, but it grants a platform—and I have resolved to use every ounce of mine to shine light on this cause. If my voice can raise a dollar for research, if my presence can bring one more woman to a screening she might have skipped, then every award I have ever won pales in comparison to that gift.

## A Call That Cannot Wait

So I ask you—not as a celebrity, but as a woman who has grieved and hoped and refused to give up—to join this fight. Schedule the mammogram you have been putting off. Learn the signs. Support the researchers working tirelessly for a cure. Walk with us, donate if you can, and above all, refuse to look away.

Early detection saves lives. Research saves lives. Community saves lives. And love—stubborn, unwavering love—is the fuel that powers all of it.

The dawn always comes. After the longest, darkest night, light returns to the world. I believe, with everything in me, that we are walking toward a morning when no woman must hear the word "cancer" as a death sentence. We are not there yet. But with every step, every dollar, every act of courage and compassion, we move closer.

I will keep walking until we arrive. I hope you will walk beside me.

*In loving memory, and in fierce hope.*

# Every Three Minutes: Why I Couldn't Look Away

*A candid conversation on awareness, action, and the power of knowing your body*

When I first heard the statistic—every three minutes, a woman in this country is diagnosed with breast cancer—I was sitting in my trailer between takes, half-listening to a morning news segment. Then the words landed. Three minutes. In the time it takes to reread a scene, someone's mother, sister, daughter, or friend receives news that will change everything.

I couldn't shake it. And I realized that for years, I'd been treating my own health as an afterthought, something to schedule "when things slow down." But things never slow down. That's the truth we all live with. So I made a decision: I would educate myself, and then I would use whatever platform I have to pass that knowledge along.

**What I Learned—and Wish I'd Known Sooner**

The first thing that surprised me was how much power we hold in our own hands, literally. Breast self-awareness isn't about performing a clinical exam in your bathroom. It's about knowing what's normal for *you*, so you notice when something changes.

Doctors I spoke with emphasized watching for lumps or thickening, of course, but also for less obvious signs: changes in skin texture, dimpling that resembles an orange peel, nipple discharge, persistent pain, or shifts in size and shape. Many of us assume breast cancer announces itself only as a lump. It doesn't always. That knowledge alone could save a life.

I began doing a monthly check, usually a few days after my period, when things are less tender. For those past menopause, choosing a consistent calendar date works just as well. The goal isn't to diagnose yourself—it's to become the expert on your own body, so you can speak up early.

**The Screenings That Matter**

Self-awareness is a starting point, not a substitute for professional care. This was the message every specialist repeated to me.

Clinical breast exams, performed by a doctor or nurse, are part of routine wellness visits. But the gold standard for early detection remains the mammogram. Guidelines vary, so I want to be honest about that—many organizations recommend women begin regular mammograms at age 40, while some suggest starting conversations earlier depending on personal risk. The key word is *conversation*. Talk to your doctor about when you should begin and how often you should go.

Risk isn't the same for everyone. A family history of breast or ovarian cancer, certain genetic markers like BRCA1 and BRCA2, and other factors can mean earlier or more frequent screening, sometimes including MRI. If cancer runs in your family, please don't wait. Ask about genetic counseling. Information is not something to fear; it's something that empowers you to make choices with your eyes open.

**Why I'm Speaking Up**

I'm an actress. I make my living pretending to be other people. But this is one role I refuse to play at a distance. Because the statistics aren't abstract—they're women I know, women I love.

Early detection dramatically improves outcomes. When breast cancer is found in its earliest, localized stage, survival rates are remarkably high. That's not a reason for complacency; it's a reason for action. Every exam, every screening, every honest conversation with a physician tips the odds in our favor.

So here's my ask. Set a reminder on your phone for a monthly self-check. Book that mammogram you've been postponing. Call the relative you've been meaning to ask about family history.

Somewhere, in the three minutes it took you to read this, another woman received a diagnosis. Let's make sure more of those diagnoses come early—when knowledge becomes the difference between fear and hope.

*Talk to your healthcare provider about the screening schedule that's right for you.*
